title: The garland-maker (44–48)
hook: who will pick the well-taught path as a skilled hand picks flowers; death carries off the one still gathering

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body like a jar, and a mind that does more than a mother can. Today, the end of the week, and chapter four: flowers.
screen: `THE BODY LIKE A JAR — MORE THAN A MOTHER CAN.`

segments.voice: Walk past a temple in India, Sri Lanka or Thailand early in the morning and you'll see the garland-makers. They sit with baskets of jasmine, marigold, lotus, and their hands move fast: choosing, threading, knotting. They don't take every flower. A skilled one can tell at a glance which bloom is fresh, which will last the day, which is already turning. Choosing well is the whole craft. The fourth chapter of the Dhammapada opens at that basket.
screen: `BASKETS OF JASMINE AND MARIGOLD.` → `HANDS CHOOSING, THREADING.` → `CHOOSING WELL IS THE CRAFT.`

segments.voice: The commentary says a group of monks, back from a journey, sat talking about the ground they'd walked over: level here, muddy there, stony, rough. The Buddha told them: that's the earth outside. Look at the earth inside you. And he spoke the chapter's first two verses. Who will master this earth, he asks, and the realms beyond it? Who will pick out the well-taught path of the dhamma, the way a skilled garland-maker picks out the right flower? The one in training will. Not the one with the most flowers, but the one who can choose. Verse forty-six adds that the body is like foam, like a mirage. Then verse forty-seven, with a hard image: “Death carries off a man who is gathering flowers and whose mind is distracted, as a flood carries off a sleeping village.” Gathering flowers, here, means collecting pleasures, one after another, never finished, never quite satisfied. Verse forty-eight says death takes that person “before he is satiated”, still reaching for the next bloom. Side by side: one person gathers endlessly and never makes a garland; the other chooses carefully and makes something. And this week you've been gathering well: appamada, heedfulness. An island. The racehorse, awake among the sleepers. Citta and the fletcher. The gatekeeper. The jar. That's a lot of flowers. The garland-maker's question is simpler: which one will you actually pick up and use?
screen: `THE EARTH OUTSIDE, THE EARTH INSIDE.` · `PICK THE PATH LIKE THE RIGHT FLOWER.` · `THE ONE STILL GATHERING.` · `THIS WEEK'S BASKET.` · then, large: `PICK THE FLOWER.`

segments.voice: Picture the week's teachings laid out in a basket: heedful is alive, make an island, awake among the sleeping, straighten the arrow, guard the mind, more than a mother can. Look them over like a garland-maker: which is fresh for you today, which fits the day you're about to have? Pick just one, let the others rest in the basket, and sit quietly with the one you chose.
The garland-maker. The skilled one who chooses the right flower from the basket, as the wise pick out the well-taught path.
Your line: pick the flower. One bloom, chosen well, from the whole basket. Day one hundred sixty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Flower garlands are among the most common Buddhist offerings, and teachers use the chapter on flowers to encourage choosing one teaching to practice rather than collecting many.

fork.setup: you've just come back from a long walk with your friends, and you're all comparing notes on the road: muddy here, rocky there. the Buddha joins you. what does he say?
options: tell me which road was best.

original.note: Pali: flower, the title of chapter four (Puppha Vagga).

trapdoor: what you thought: 'gathering flowers' in verse forty-seven is a sweet, innocent picture.
what it means: it's collecting pleasures endlessly, never satisfied, and death arrives mid-gathering.
what a scholar hears: verses 44–45 turn on 'dhammapadam sudesitam' and 'kusalo pupphamiva pacessati': the well-taught dhammapada, picked as a skilled one picks a flower.

chat.says: We've heard so many teachings this week. What do I do with them all?
options: Pick one and use it, like a garland-maker choosing a fresh flower.
Collect as many as you can; more flowers means more wisdom.
Memorize them all first, then decide which to practice.
chat.meaning: The skilled garland-maker chooses well; the one gathering endlessly is carried off unsatisfied. Pick the teaching you'll actually use.

dhamma.meaning: the teaching, and the way things truly are

Citta.meaning: mind, the heart-mind that thinks, feels and wants
